questions.title: What requires_grad=True Actually Builds
questions.prompt: A teammate asks why setting requires_grad=True on a tensor is enough for PyTorch to later compute gradients with a single .backward() call, with no explicit derivative written anywhere in the code. Explain what actually happens under the hood.
questions.modelAnswer: Setting requires_grad=True does not compute anything by itself; it tells PyTorch to track every subsequent operation performed on that tensor so it can build a computational graph dynamically as the forward pass runs. Every operation (add, matmul, relu, etc.) applied to a tracked tensor produces a new tensor that stores a grad_fn pointing back to the operation and its inputs. By the time the forward pass reaches a scalar loss, PyTorch has an entire directed graph connecting that loss back to every leaf tensor that had requires_grad=True. Calling .backward() walks that graph in reverse using the chain rule, computing the local derivative at each node and multiplying it into the gradient flowing from downstream, and accumulates the final result into each leaf tensor's .grad attribute. No derivative is 'written' anywhere because each built-in PyTorch operation already knows its own local derivative rule; autograd's job is purely to compose those known rules correctly along the exact path the data actually took.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as PyTorch keeping a receipt of every operation as it happens, not computing gradients up front. requires_grad=True just flips a tracking flag; from that point on, every op you do on that tensor gets a grad_fn attached that remembers what produced it and from what. Once you reach your scalar loss, you've built a whole graph without meaning to -- it was assembled automatically by just doing normal math. .backward() then walks that graph backward, applying the chain rule at each step, because each individual op (matmul, relu, add) already has a known local derivative baked into PyTorch. So the 'magic' isn't that PyTorch knows calculus about your model specifically -- it's that it knows calculus about each primitive operation, and autograd just chains those known pieces together in the right order.
questions.example: x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True); y = x**2 + 3*x; y.backward() sets x.grad to 2*x+3 = 7, computed by chaining the known derivative of power and addition, not by PyTorch deriving y's formula symbolically ahead of time.
commonMistakes: Thinking requires_grad=True immediately computes a gradient instead of just enabling tracking
Believing PyTorch symbolically derives the whole formula in advance rather than composing per-operation local derivatives at backward time
Forgetting that only leaf tensors with requires_grad=True accumulate a .grad -- intermediate tensors don't retain .grad by default
Assuming the graph is static and reused across iterations instead of rebuilt fresh on every forward pass
keyPoints: requires_grad=True enables tracking, it does not compute gradients itself
Each operation on a tracked tensor attaches a grad_fn recording how it was produced
The computational graph is built dynamically during the forward pass
backward() applies the chain rule using each primitive operation's known local derivative
Gradients accumulate into leaf tensors' .grad attribute

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains requires_grad as enabling tracking, not computing gradients
Describes the dynamic graph built via grad_fn during the forward pass
Explains backward() as chain rule composition over known local derivatives
Clear, accurate, appropriately scoped explanation

questions.title: Why Gradients Accumulate Instead of Reset
questions.prompt: A junior engineer's training loop calls loss.backward() every step but never calls optimizer.zero_grad(). After a few steps, training diverges wildly. Explain exactly why this happens.
questions.modelAnswer: PyTorch's .grad attribute accumulates by design rather than resetting automatically on every backward() call, because this behavior is what makes gradient accumulation across multiple mini-batches possible for cases that genuinely want it (e.g. simulating a larger batch size on limited memory). When zero_grad() is never called, each backward() call adds the newly computed gradient on top of whatever was already sitting in .grad from the previous step, so by step three a parameter's .grad attribute holds the sum of three steps' worth of gradients, not just the current one. The optimizer then applies an update scaled to that inflated gradient, taking a much larger step than intended. Because this compounds every iteration, the effective step size grows roughly linearly with the step count, which is exactly the kind of runaway behavior that produces diverging loss, exploding weights, and eventually NaNs within a handful of steps.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it mechanically: .grad doesn't zero itself out between calls, it adds to whatever's already there, because that's genuinely useful for people who want to accumulate gradients across micro-batches on purpose. The problem here is nobody is doing that on purpose -- they just forgot the zero_grad() call. So step one's gradient lands in .grad, step two's gradient gets added on top of that instead of replacing it, step three adds a third layer on top of that, and the optimizer is now applying updates sized for triple the real gradient. That's a recipe for divergence almost immediately, because the effective learning rate is silently growing every single step. The fix is one line -- optimizer.zero_grad() before backward() each iteration -- but I'd also mention that this is exactly the kind of bug that's easy to miss because the code runs without erroring, it just slowly blows up, which is why it's worth knowing the mechanism cold rather than just memorizing 'always call zero_grad.'
questions.example:
for x, y in loader:
    # missing: optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
commonMistakes: Assuming .grad automatically resets between backward() calls
Not recognizing that this produces a slowly compounding, not immediately crashing, failure
Confusing this bug with a learning-rate-too-high bug when diagnosing, missing the real cause
Not knowing that gradient accumulation (skipping zero_grad on purpose for several steps) is a legitimate, different technique
keyPoints: By design, .grad accumulates across backward() calls rather than resetting
Missing zero_grad() causes gradients from prior steps to stack on top of the current step's gradient
The effective step size grows roughly with the number of steps since the last zero_grad()
This produces progressive divergence rather than an immediate crash, making it a subtle bug
zero_grad() before backward() each iteration is the fix; intentional accumulation is a separate, deliberate technique

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that .grad accumulates by design
Explains the compounding effect across steps and why it causes divergence
Identifies the fix (zero_grad before backward)
Notes the distinction from intentional gradient accumulation

questions.title: nn.Module and Where Parameters Actually Live
questions.prompt: Explain what subclassing nn.Module actually gives you beyond organizing code into a class -- specifically, how PyTorch finds all the learnable parameters of a model you define this way without you ever registering them manually.
questions.modelAnswer: nn.Module provides more than organization -- it overrides Python's normal attribute-setting behavior (via __setattr__) so that whenever you assign a submodule or an nn.Parameter to an attribute inside __init__, the module automatically registers it in internal dictionaries (_modules and _parameters) rather than treating it like an ordinary Python attribute. That registration is what lets model.parameters() recursively walk every submodule's own registered parameters and yield a flat iterator over every learnable tensor in the whole model, which is exactly what gets handed to an optimizer. Nothing about this is automatic from Python's perspective; it is nn.Module's own bookkeeping that makes 'define layers as attributes' equivalent to 'register all their parameters for training.' If you instead store a layer in a plain Python list or dict instead of an nn.ModuleList/nn.ModuleDict, this registration breaks silently -- the layer still runs in forward(), but its parameters never show up in model.parameters(), so the optimizer never updates them.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say the real trick is in __setattr__, not in __init__. When you write self.fc1 = nn.Linear(...) inside your module's __init__, nn.Module intercepts that assignment and files nn.Linear's parameters away in an internal registry instead of just setting a normal attribute. That's the entire reason model.parameters() can walk the whole model and hand every learnable tensor to your optimizer without you manually listing each one. I'd also flag the classic gotcha here, because I've hit it myself: if you put a bunch of layers in a plain Python list instead of nn.ModuleList, forward() still works fine because you can still index into the list and call the layers -- but none of those layers' parameters get registered, so your optimizer silently never updates them. It doesn't error, it just quietly doesn't train that part of the network, which makes it a nasty one to debug.
questions.example:
self.layers = [nn.Linear(10, 10) for _ in range(3)]  # BROKEN: parameters invisible to optimizer
self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(10, 10) for _ in range(3)])  # correct: registered
commonMistakes: Thinking nn.Module parameter discovery is just Python introspection rather than nn.Module's own __setattr__ override
Storing submodules in a plain list/dict instead of nn.ModuleList/nn.ModuleDict, silently breaking parameter registration
Assuming a broken registration will raise an error rather than just fail to train that part of the model
Not realizing model.parameters() recurses through all nested submodules automatically
keyPoints: nn.Module overrides attribute assignment to auto-register submodules and parameters
model.parameters() recursively collects every registered parameter across submodules
Storing layers in a plain Python list/dict breaks registration silently
nn.ModuleList/nn.ModuleDict exist specifically to preserve registration for collections of layers
A broken registration still runs in forward() but never gets optimized

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains __setattr__-based automatic parameter registration

Clear and accurate overall

questions.title: Cross-Entropy vs. MSE: Picking the Right Loss
questions.prompt: A teammate uses mean squared error (MSE) loss for a 10-class image classification model and finds training is slow and accuracy plateaus low. Explain why MSE is a poor fit here and why cross-entropy is the standard choice.
questions.modelAnswer: MSE treats the model's output as a continuous numeric target and penalizes squared distance, which is a poor match for classification where the target is a categorical label, not a point on a number line -- MSE has no way to express 'this class is simply wrong' versus 'this class is numerically close,' and classes 3 and 7 aren't actually closer or farther apart than classes 3 and 9. More concretely, MSE combined with a softmax output produces very flat gradients when the prediction is confidently wrong, because the squared-error gradient shrinks as the sigmoid/softmax output saturates near 0 or 1 -- exactly when you need the strongest correction signal. Cross-entropy, by contrast, is derived directly from the likelihood of the correct class under the model's predicted probability distribution, and its gradient with respect to the logits (when paired with softmax) simplifies to simply (predicted_probability - true_label), which stays large exactly when the model is confidently wrong and shrinks smoothly as the prediction becomes correct. That is the mathematical reason cross-entropy trains faster and converges to better accuracy on classification tasks than MSE.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core issue is that MSE is built for regression, where the target really is a number on a line and being '2 away' is twice as bad as being '1 away.' That doesn't describe classification at all -- there's no sense in which predicting class 7 instead of class 3 is numerically closer than predicting class 9, so MSE is optimizing toward a geometric structure that doesn't exist in the label space. The gradient problem makes it worse in practice: once the softmax output saturates near 0 or 1 for a confidently wrong prediction, MSE's gradient through that saturated unit gets tiny, so the model barely gets corrected exactly when it most needs correcting. Cross-entropy sidesteps this because it comes straight from maximum likelihood on the predicted probability distribution, and its gradient with softmax reduces to just predicted-minus-true, which stays strong on confident wrong answers and only shrinks once the model is actually getting it right. That's why switching the loss function alone, with nothing else changed, usually fixes both the slow training and the low accuracy plateau the teammate is seeing.
questions.example: For true label 3 and softmax output [0.05]*10 except 0.55 for class 3, cross-entropy gradient on the correct logit is 0.55-1=-0.45 (strong pull); MSE's gradient through the saturated softmax units is much smaller in magnitude for wrong classes near 0.
commonMistakes: Treating class labels as if they have numeric distance that MSE can meaningfully penalize
Not recognizing MSE's vanishing-gradient problem at saturated softmax outputs
Forgetting cross-entropy is derived from maximum likelihood on the predicted class distribution
Assuming any loss function will work equally well as long as training eventually converges
keyPoints: MSE assumes a numeric target space, which doesn't describe categorical class labels
MSE's gradient through a saturated softmax is small exactly when correction is most needed
Cross-entropy is derived from maximum likelihood on the predicted probability distribution
Cross-entropy's gradient with softmax simplifies to predicted-minus-true, staying strong on confident errors
Switching from MSE to cross-entropy on classification tasks typically improves both speed and final accuracy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why MSE is a poor fit for categorical labels
Correctly explains the vanishing-gradient issue with MSE on saturated outputs
Explains cross-entropy's maximum-likelihood derivation and gradient behavior
Clear, accurate explanation overall

questions.title: What Query, Key, and Value Actually Represent in Self-Attention
questions.prompt: A new team member can recite that self-attention uses 'queries, keys, and values' but admits they don't actually understand what those three things represent or why you need three separate projections instead of one. Give them a real explanation.
questions.modelAnswer: Each input token's embedding is linearly projected three separate ways using three separate learned weight matrices, producing a query vector, a key vector, and a value vector for that token -- the same underlying embedding, viewed through three different learned lenses. The query represents what this position is 'looking for' from other positions; the key represents what each position 'advertises' about itself as being relevant for; and the value represents the actual content that gets passed forward if that position is attended to. Attention scores are computed as the dot product of one position's query against every position's key, which measures how well what position A is looking for matches what position B is advertising -- high dot product means strong relevance. Those scores are scaled and passed through softmax to get attention weights that sum to 1, and the output for position A is the weighted sum of every position's value vector, weighted by how relevant A found each one. The reason you need three separate projections rather than one is that 'what I'm looking for' and 'what I advertise' and 'what I actually contain' are functionally different roles that the same token's content needs to play simultaneously, and giving each role its own learned projection lets the model learn each role independently rather than forcing one fixed representation to serve all three jobs at once.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd use a search-engine analogy because it maps almost exactly: query is like your search box -- what you're looking for right now. Key is like the index terms on every document -- what each document says it's about, which your query gets compared against. Value is the actual document content you get back once a match is found. The reason you need three separate learned projections of the same token embedding, instead of reusing one, is that those are three genuinely different jobs: 'what am I looking for,' 'what do I advertise,' and 'what do I actually contain' aren't the same thing, even for the same word. Mechanically, you take the dot product of a token's query against every token's key to get a relevance score per pair, softmax those scores so they sum to one, and then use those weights to blend everyone's value vectors into the output for that position. The query-key dot product is literally the 'how relevant is this to what I'm looking for' computation, and the value is what actually flows through once relevance is established.
questions.example: Q = X @ W_q, K = X @ W_k, V = X @ W_v; attention_weights = softmax(Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k)); output = attention_weights @ V -- three separate learned matrices W_q, W_k, W_v applied to the same input X.
commonMistakes: Describing Q, K, V as arbitrary labels without explaining what role each actually plays
Not explaining that all three come from the same input embedding via three different learned projections
Forgetting that the query-key dot product is what produces the relevance/attention score
Confusing the value vector (what gets passed forward) with the key vector (what gets matched against)
keyPoints: Query, key, and value are three separate learned linear projections of the same token embedding
Query represents what a position is looking for; key represents what a position advertises
Value represents the content that actually gets passed forward when attended to
Attention scores come from the query-key dot product, scaled and softmaxed into weights
Three separate roles need three separate projections because they are functionally different jobs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what query, key, and value each represent
Explains the dot-product-then-softmax mechanism for computing attention weights
Explains why three separate projections are needed rather than one
Clear and well-structured explanation

questions.title: Why Transformers Replaced RNNs for Sequence Modeling
questions.prompt: Explain the two main practical reasons self-attention-based transformers displaced RNNs/LSTMs as the dominant architecture for sequence modeling, beyond just 'they perform better.'
questions.modelAnswer: The first reason is parallelism: an RNN processes a sequence strictly step by step, since each hidden state depends on the previous hidden state, which means training cannot parallelize across the time dimension and GPU utilization suffers badly on long sequences. Self-attention computes relationships between all token pairs in a sequence simultaneously via matrix multiplication, so the entire sequence can be processed in parallel during training, which is a dramatically better fit for modern GPU hardware and is a major reason transformers scale so much more efficiently to large datasets and large models. The second reason is long-range dependency handling: RNNs/LSTMs propagate information through a chain of hidden states, so a dependency between tokens far apart in the sequence has to survive many sequential transformations, and in practice this information degrades (the vanishing gradient problem during training, and signal degradation during the forward pass itself) even with LSTM's gating mechanisms designed to mitigate it. Self-attention connects any two positions directly in a single operation regardless of their distance in the sequence, so a dependency between token 1 and token 500 costs exactly the same computational path as a dependency between adjacent tokens, which empirically produces much more reliable long-range modeling.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point to two things, not one. First, pure training speed: RNNs are inherently sequential, each step needs the previous hidden state, so you can't parallelize across time during training, and that's a brutal bottleneck on modern GPUs which are built for massive parallel matrix math, not step-by-step loops. Self-attention is just matrix multiplications across the whole sequence at once, so it uses the hardware the way it's meant to be used, and that alone made training on much larger datasets practical. Second, long-range dependencies: an RNN has to carry information forward through every single intermediate step in a chain, and even with LSTM gating, that signal degrades over long distances -- it's the vanishing gradient problem showing up as a modeling limitation, not just a training nuisance. Self-attention just connects any two tokens directly, in one hop, no matter how far apart they are in the sequence, so a relationship between the first and five-hundredth token is exactly as easy to represent as one between adjacent tokens. Put together, you get an architecture that trains faster on the hardware you actually have and models long sequences more reliably -- that combination, not just raw benchmark numbers, is why RNNs lost out.
questions.example: Translating a long sentence where the subject at position 1 determines verb agreement at position 40: an RNN must propagate that signal through 39 sequential hidden-state updates; self-attention connects position 1 to position 40 in a single dot-product computation.
commonMistakes: Giving only a vague 'transformers perform better' answer without a mechanistic reason
Not mentioning the parallelization advantage over sequential RNN computation
Not explaining why long-range dependencies specifically degrade in RNNs even with LSTM gating
Confusing attention's computational cost (quadratic in sequence length) with RNN's sequential bottleneck -- these are different tradeoffs
keyPoints: RNNs process sequences step by step, which prevents parallelizing across the time dimension during training
Self-attention computes all pairwise token relationships simultaneously via matrix multiplication
RNNs propagate long-range dependencies through many sequential hidden-state updates, which degrades signal
Self-attention connects any two positions directly in one step regardless of distance
The combination of better hardware utilization and more reliable long-range modeling drove the shift

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the parallelization advantage of self-attention over sequential RNNs
Explains the long-range dependency advantage of direct attention connections
Avoids a vague 'just performs better' answer

questions.title: Why Transformers Need Positional Encoding at All
questions.prompt: Someone asks why transformers need an explicit positional encoding step when RNNs never needed anything like it. Explain the underlying reason.
questions.modelAnswer: RNNs process tokens strictly in sequence order, so position is implicitly encoded by the order of computation itself -- the hidden state at step 5 was necessarily computed after steps 1 through 4, so sequence order is baked into the architecture's execution. Self-attention has no such structural ordering: the attention computation between any two tokens is a symmetric function of their content (query and key vectors) with no reference to where each token sits in the sequence, so if you shuffled the token order and recomputed attention with no positional information, you would get a mathematically permutation-invariant result -- the model literally cannot tell 'the cat sat' from 'sat the cat' from content alone. Positional encoding fixes this by injecting a signal that depends on each token's position into its embedding before attention is computed, commonly by adding a fixed sinusoidal pattern (where the specific sinusoid frequencies vary across embedding dimensions, giving every position a mathematically unique signature) or a learned positional embedding, so that position becomes part of the content attention is matching on. Without it, a transformer would process sequences as unordered sets, which would make it fundamentally incapable of representing word order, syntax, or any order-dependent meaning.
questions.professionalAnswer: The short version is that self-attention is permutation-invariant by construction -- it has no built-in sense of order at all, unlike an RNN where order is baked into the architecture because step 5 literally can't be computed before step 4. If you fed a transformer's attention mechanism a shuffled sentence with the exact same tokens, it would compute the exact same attention pattern, because attention only looks at content (query/key similarity), never position. That's a real problem because word order carries meaning -- 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' have the same tokens in a different order and very different meanings. Positional encoding is the fix: you inject a position-dependent signal into each token's embedding before attention runs, often a fixed sinusoidal pattern with different frequencies across the embedding's dimensions, so every position gets a unique signature baked into its vector. Once that's added, attention can effectively use position as part of what it's matching on, even though the attention math itself never explicitly 'knows' about order -- it's smuggled in through the input representation instead of the mechanism.
questions.example: Without positional encoding, 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' would produce identical sets of token embeddings fed into attention, since both sentences contain the same multiset of tokens -- the model has no way to distinguish them.
commonMistakes: Not realizing self-attention is permutation-invariant without positional information
Assuming position is somehow implicit in the attention mechanism itself
Describing positional encoding as optional or purely cosmetic rather than structurally necessary
Confusing positional encoding with the embedding layer itself rather than an additive signal on top of it
keyPoints: RNNs encode position implicitly through sequential computation order
Self-attention is permutation-invariant with respect to content alone
Without positional information, shuffled-order input would produce identical attention results
Positional encoding injects a position-dependent signal into each token's embedding before attention
This is structurally necessary, not optional, for a transformer to represent word order

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why self-attention is permutation-invariant without positional information
Contrasts this correctly with RNNs' implicit ordering

questions.title: The Core Components of a Markov Decision Process
questions.prompt: Explain the components of a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and why the 'Markov' property -- that the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the full history -- matters for how RL algorithms are designed.
questions.modelAnswer: An MDP is formally defined by a set of states S, a set of actions A, a transition function (or distribution) P(s'|s,a) describing the probability of reaching state s' given current state s and action a, a reward function R(s,a,s') specifying the immediate reward received, and a discount factor gamma that controls how much future reward is valued relative to immediate reward. A policy is a mapping from states to actions (or a distribution over actions), and the value function estimates the expected cumulative discounted reward obtainable from a given state (or state-action pair) under a given policy. The Markov property -- that P(s'|s,a) depends only on the current state and action, not on the sequence of states and actions that preceded it -- matters enormously because it is what makes the state a sufficient statistic for decision-making: an agent never needs to remember the full history of everything that happened, only the current state, to act optimally. This is precisely what allows value functions and the Bellman equation to be defined recursively in terms of the current state alone, which is the mathematical foundation nearly every RL algorithm (value iteration, Q-learning, policy gradients) relies on. If the environment were not Markovian, an agent would in principle need to condition on arbitrarily long history to act optimally, which breaks the clean recursive structure these algorithms depend on.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lay out the five pieces: states, actions, a transition function describing what happens when you take an action in a state, a reward function, and a discount factor that trades off immediate versus future reward. On top of that sits a policy, which just maps states to actions, and a value function, which estimates how much cumulative reward you can expect from here on if you follow a given policy. The Markov property is the part that actually makes all of this tractable -- it says the next state only depends on your current state and action, not on the whole history that got you there. That matters because it means the current state alone is enough information to make an optimal decision; you don't need to remember everything that happened five steps ago. That's exactly what lets you write the Bellman equation recursively in terms of the current state, and basically every RL algorithm I'd mention after this -- Q-learning, policy gradients, actor-critic -- is built on top of that recursive structure being valid. If an environment weren't Markovian, you'd technically need to track arbitrarily long history to act optimally, which is a much harder problem than what these algorithms are designed to solve.
questions.example: In chess, the current board position is (approximately) Markovian -- the best next move depends on the board as it stands, not on the specific sequence of moves that produced it (ignoring repetition-draw rules), which is why chess engines can evaluate a position without replaying its full history.

Not connecting the Markov property to why algorithms like the Bellman equation are even well-defined

A policy maps states to actions; a value function estimates expected cumulative discounted reward
The Markov property means the next state depends only on the current state and action
This property makes the current state a sufficient statistic, enabling recursive value functions
Nearly all RL algorithms rely on this recursive (Bellman) structure being valid

questions.title: Why Pure Exploitation Fails in Reinforcement Learning
questions.prompt: A teammate's RL agent always picks the action with the highest currently-estimated reward (pure exploitation). Explain why this almost always leads to a suboptimal policy, and what exploration does to fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: An agent's reward estimates for each action are built from limited experience, so early on they are noisy and can easily be wrong -- an action that happens to look worse in the first few tries might actually be the best action, and pure exploitation will never discover this because it never tries that action again once it looks slightly worse than an alternative. This is the classic exploration-exploitation tradeoff: exploitation means acting on current best knowledge to maximize immediate expected reward, while exploration means deliberately trying actions that don't currently look best, purely to gather more information that could improve future decisions. Pure exploitation converges prematurely to whichever action looked good by chance early on, and then that estimate never gets corrected because the agent stops gathering new data about the alternatives. Exploration strategies (epsilon-greedy, which picks a random action some fraction of the time; or more sophisticated methods like upper-confidence-bound approaches that explicitly favor actions with high uncertainty) counteract this by continuing to sample alternatives even after a seemingly-best action is found, so the agent's reward estimates keep improving and it doesn't get permanently stuck on an early, possibly incorrect, local optimum.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem is that your reward estimates are only as good as the data you've collected so far, and early on, that data is thin and noisy. If you always exploit -- just pick whatever currently looks best -- you can get unlucky: the actual best action might look mediocre in its first couple of tries purely by chance, and a pure-exploitation agent will never go back and try it again once something else looks even slightly better. It locks in on whatever happened to look good early and never collects the data that would correct that mistake. That's the whole point of the exploration-exploitation tradeoff: exploitation maximizes reward given what you currently believe, exploration deliberately spends some reward now to learn something that improves future decisions. The fix is simple in concept -- something like epsilon-greedy, where you take a random action some small percentage of the time no matter what your current estimates say, so you keep gathering information on actions you'd otherwise have written off. More sophisticated approaches like upper-confidence-bound methods go further and specifically target actions you're most uncertain about, rather than exploring uniformly at random. Either way, the core idea is the same: without some ongoing exploration, your agent's knowledge stops improving and it can get permanently stuck on a false 'best' action.
questions.example: A slot-machine (bandit) with 3 arms where arm A's first 2 pulls happen to return low reward by chance despite having the best true average -- pure exploitation abandons arm A forever after 2 pulls; epsilon-greedy keeps occasionally revisiting it and eventually discovers it's actually best.

questions.title: Why LLMs Need a Learned Reward Model Instead of a Hand-Written Reward Function
questions.prompt: In classic RL, reward functions are often hand-written (e.g. +1 for reaching a goal, -1 for a collision). Explain why aligning an LLM's behavior to something like 'be helpful and harmless' can't just use a hand-written reward function the same way, and why a learned reward model is used instead.
questions.modelAnswer: A hand-written reward function works when the desired outcome can be specified as a simple, checkable function of the environment's state -- 'did the robot reach the goal coordinates' is objectively checkable. 'Is this response helpful and harmless' has no such checkable formula: helpfulness and harmlessness are holistic, context-dependent human judgments about open-ended text that cannot be reduced to a short hand-codeable rule without either being trivially gameable (e.g. a hand-written rule like 'reward longer responses' gets exploited into padded, unhelpful verbosity) or missing most of what actually matters. The solution used in RLHF is to replace the hand-written reward function with a learned reward model: humans compare pairs of model outputs and indicate which one they prefer, that preference data is used to train a separate neural network (the reward model) to predict a scalar score that reflects human preference, and that learned reward model's output is then used as the reward signal for an RL algorithm (typically PPO) to fine-tune the language model's policy. This effectively outsources the impossible task of hand-specifying 'helpful and harmless' to a model trained directly on examples of human judgment, which can capture far more nuance than any rule a person could write down directly, though it introduces its own risks since the reward model is itself an imperfect proxy for true human preference that can be over-optimized against (reward hacking).
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer is that nobody can write down a formula for 'helpful and harmless' the way you can write down 'did the robot's coordinates match the goal.' Any rule you try to hand-code either misses most of what people actually mean by helpful, or gets gamed immediately -- reward longer answers and you get bloated, padded responses; reward confident-sounding answers and you get confidently wrong ones. So instead of trying to hand-specify the reward, RLHF trains a separate model to approximate human judgment directly: you show people pairs of model outputs, they say which one they prefer, and you train a reward model on that preference data to output a score that tracks what humans actually tend to prefer. Then that learned reward model becomes the reward signal an RL algorithm, usually PPO, optimizes the language model against. It's a genuinely clever workaround for a problem that doesn't have a clean mathematical specification -- you're learning the reward function from data instead of writing it by hand. The tradeoff I'd be honest about is that the reward model is still just an imperfect proxy for real human preference, and if you optimize against it too hard, the policy can learn to exploit quirks of the reward model itself rather than genuinely becoming more helpful -- that's reward hacking, and it's a real, ongoing concern in how these systems are trained.
questions.example: A hand-written rule 'reward +1 per helpful-sounding keyword like 'certainly' or 'here's how'' would be gamed almost immediately by a policy that stuffs those words into every response regardless of actual helpfulness -- which is exactly the kind of gap a learned reward model trained on real human comparisons is meant to close.

Not explaining the human preference-comparison data collection process behind reward models
Treating the learned reward model as a perfect substitute for human judgment rather than an imperfect proxy
Forgetting to mention that the reward model's output becomes the signal for a downstream RL step (typically PPO)

Hand-written reward proxies for open-ended behavior are easily gamed

questions.title: Writing a Correct Minimal PyTorch Training Loop
questions.prompt: Write a correct, minimal training loop in PyTorch for a regression model given a model, a DataLoader, an optimizer, and MSE loss, making sure all the standard steps are present and in the right order.
questions.code:
model = MLP(in_dim=10, hidden=64, out_dim=1)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = torch.nn.MSELoss()
questions.modelAnswer: A correct training loop must, for every batch: zero the gradients before the backward pass, run the forward pass, compute the loss, call backward() to populate gradients, then call optimizer.step() to apply the update -- in that exact order, with zero_grad() happening before backward() each iteration so gradients from the previous step don't accumulate. Any missing or reordered step produces a bug: skipping zero_grad() causes gradient accumulation, calling step() before backward() applies a stale or empty gradient, and computing loss before the forward pass is simply impossible since loss depends on the model's output.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it as: loop over epochs, loop over batches from the DataLoader, zero_grad, forward pass to get predictions, compute the loss against the targets, backward to get gradients, then step to apply the update. The order matters a lot here -- zero_grad has to come before backward, and step has to come after backward, or the update either double-counts old gradients or applies nothing at all.
questions.example:
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    for x, y in dataloader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        preds = model(x)
        loss = loss_fn(preds, y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    print(f"epoch {epoch} loss {loss.item():.4f}")
commonMistakes: Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad(), causing gradient accumulation across steps
Calling optimizer.step() before loss.backward(), applying a stale gradient
Computing the loss with mismatched prediction/target shapes without checking
Not calling .item() when logging loss, accidentally keeping the whole computation graph alive and leaking memory
keyPoints: Order must be: zero_grad, forward, compute loss, backward, step
zero_grad() must run before backward() each iteration to prevent gradient accumulation
backward() must run before step() so the optimizer has a current gradient to apply
Loss should be detached (.item()) when logged to avoid retaining the computation graph

questions.title: Fixing Gradient Accumulation Caused by a Missing zero_grad
questions.prompt: The following training loop diverges after a few steps. Find and fix the bug.
questions.code:
for x, y in dataloader:
    preds = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(preds, y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
questions.modelAnswer: The loop never calls optimizer.zero_grad(), so gradients from every prior step accumulate into .grad on top of the current step's gradient, producing an effectively growing update size each iteration until the loss diverges. The fix is to call optimizer.zero_grad() at the start of each iteration, before backward() is called.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic missing zero_grad bug -- each backward() call adds to the existing .grad instead of replacing it, so the effective gradient magnitude keeps growing step over step. The fix is one line: call optimizer.zero_grad() before the forward/backward pass in each iteration.
questions.example:
for x, y in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    preds = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(preds, y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

Calling zero_grad() on the model instead of the optimizer (works if parameters match, but is non-standard)

Not verifying the fix by checking that .grad magnitude stays stable across steps after the change

questions.title: Computing Scaled Dot-Product Self-Attention by Hand in PyTorch
questions.prompt: Write the core scaled dot-product self-attention computation in PyTorch given query, key, and value tensors of shape (batch, seq_len, d_k).
questions.code:
Q = torch.randn(2, 5, 16)
K = torch.randn(2, 5, 16)
V = torch.randn(2, 5, 16)
questions.modelAnswer: The computation is: scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2,-1), scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k) to prevent the dot products from growing too large in magnitude as d_k increases (which would push softmax into a saturated, near-one-hot regime with vanishing gradients), then softmax over the last dimension to get attention weights, then multiply those weights by V to get the output. The scaling factor is essential, not cosmetic -- without it, larger d_k values systematically produce larger-magnitude dot products purely due to dimensionality, independent of actual relevance, which destabilizes training.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write scores as Q times K transposed on the last two dimensions, divide by the square root of d_k to keep the scale sane regardless of the embedding dimension, softmax that over the key dimension to get weights that sum to one per query, then multiply those weights by V. I'd flag the scaling step specifically in an interview, because it's easy to forget and the model will technically still run without it -- it just trains worse, because unscaled dot products grow with d_k and push softmax toward a near-one-hot, low-gradient regime.
questions.example:
import math
scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])
weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
output = weights @ V  # shape (2, 5, 16)
commonMistakes: Forgetting the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling factor entirely
Applying softmax over the wrong dimension (should be over the key/seq dimension, the last axis of scores)
Transposing the wrong two dimensions of K, breaking the matmul shape
Not handling batch dimensions correctly when extending beyond a single example
keyPoints: scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2,-1), scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k)

questions.title: Building a Simple MLP as an nn.Module
questions.prompt: Write a two-hidden-layer MLP as a correct nn.Module subclass, with ReLU activations, for a 20-dimensional input and 3-class classification output.
questions.modelAnswer: The class must call super().__init__() first so nn.Module's own initialization (setting up the internal parameter/module registries) runs before any layers are assigned, then assign each layer as a direct attribute (not inside a plain list) so they register correctly, and define forward() to specify the actual computation order including activations, since defining layers in __init__ says nothing about how data flows through them. Raw logits (no softmax) should be returned from forward() when used with nn.CrossEntropyLoss, since that loss function applies log-softmax internally.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd subclass nn.Module, call super().__init__() first thing, then define three linear layers as direct attributes -- 20 to a hidden size, hidden to hidden, hidden to 3 classes -- with ReLU in between in forward(). I'd deliberately not put a softmax at the end, since nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits and applies log-softmax internally; adding softmax here would double-apply it if paired with that loss.
questions.example:
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim=20, hidden=64, num_classes=3):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_dim, hidden)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden, hidden)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(hidden, num_classes)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = self.relu(self.fc2(x))
        return self.fc3(x)  # raw logits, no softmax

Applying softmax in forward() when using it with nn.CrossEntropyLoss, which already applies log-softmax
Storing layers in a plain list instead of as direct attributes or nn.ModuleList
Omitting activation functions between layers, making the model equivalent to a single linear transform

questions.title: Writing a Custom Dataset and DataLoader

questions.modelAnswer: A custom Dataset subclass must implement __len__ (returning the total number of samples) and __getitem__ (returning a single sample given an index, converted to tensors), and must not load the entire dataset into memory unnecessarily if it can be avoided for large datasets -- though for small in-memory numpy arrays, storing them directly is fine. The DataLoader then handles batching, shuffling, and (optionally) parallel loading via worker processes, so none of that logic needs to be written manually.

questions.title: Saving and Loading a Model Checkpoint Correctly
questions.prompt: Write code to correctly save a model and optimizer checkpoint mid-training, and reload it to resume training from the same point.
questions.modelAnswer: A correct checkpoint for resuming training must save the model's state_dict, the optimizer's state_dict (which holds per-parameter state like Adam's momentum terms -- without it, resuming would reset momentum and effectively change the optimization trajectory), and the current epoch/step number, not just the raw model weights. Loading requires constructing a model and optimizer with the same architecture and hyperparameters first, then calling load_state_dict() on each, and calling model.train() afterward if resuming training (versus model.eval() if only running inference), since some layers like BatchNorm and Dropout behave differently in each mode.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd save a dict containing the model's state_dict, the optimizer's state_dict, and the epoch number -- not just torch.save(model), which only saves weights and would silently reset the optimizer's internal state like Adam's momentum when you resume. To reload, I construct the model and optimizer architecture exactly as before, then call load_state_dict on both from the saved dict, and explicitly call model.train() if I'm resuming training, since layers like BatchNorm and Dropout behave differently in train versus eval mode and I don't want to accidentally resume in eval mode.
questions.example:
torch.save({
    "epoch": epoch,
    "model_state_dict": model.state_dict(),
    "optimizer_state_dict": optimizer.state_dict(),
}, "checkpoint.pt")

checkpoint = torch.load("checkpoint.pt")
model.load_state_dict(checkpoint["model_state_dict"])
optimizer.load_state_dict(checkpoint["optimizer_state_dict"])
start_epoch = checkpoint["epoch"] + 1
model.train()

questions.title: Setting Seeds for Reproducible Training Runs
questions.prompt: Write the setup code needed at the start of a training script to make results as reproducible as possible across runs on the same hardware.
questions.modelAnswer: Full reproducibility requires seeding every source of randomness independently, since setting only one library's seed leaves the others uncontrolled: Python's own random module, numpy's random generator, and PyTorch's CPU and CUDA random generators all need explicit seeds. Additionally, some GPU operations (particularly certain convolution algorithms chosen by cuDNN's auto-tuner) are nondeterministic by default for performance reasons, so torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic should be set True and benchmark set False to force deterministic algorithm selection, at some cost to speed. DataLoader worker processes also have their own separate random state that needs seeding via a worker_init_fn if using multiple workers with random augmentation, or results can still vary run to run despite seeding everything else.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd seed everything, not just one thing, because each library maintains its own independent random state: random.seed(), numpy's np.random.seed(), and torch.manual_seed() plus torch.cuda.manual_seed_all() for GPU. I'd also explicitly set torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True and cudnn.benchmark = False, because cuDNN's default behavior picks the fastest convolution algorithm it can find, which isn't always deterministic -- that's a sneaky source of non-reproducibility people often miss even after seeding everything else. If I'm using a DataLoader with multiple workers and any randomness in my augmentation pipeline, I'd also pass a worker_init_fn that seeds each worker's own random state deterministically based on its worker id, because worker processes don't automatically inherit the main process's seed.
questions.example:
import random, numpy as np, torch

def set_seed(seed=42):
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False

set_seed(42)

questions.title: Applying Gradient Clipping in a Training Loop
questions.prompt: Add gradient clipping to a training loop to stabilize training against occasional exploding-gradient spikes.
questions.code:
for x, y in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    preds = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(preds, y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
questions.modelAnswer: Gradient clipping must be applied after backward() has computed the gradients but before optimizer.step() applies them, since clipping operates directly on the .grad values that step() would otherwise use unmodified. torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ rescales the entire gradient vector (across all parameters together, not per-parameter) if its total norm exceeds a specified maximum, which caps the size of any single update without changing its direction, preventing a rare large-gradient spike from catastrophically disrupting the model's weights in one step.
questions.professionalAnswer: The clip call goes in exactly one place: after loss.backward() and before optimizer.step(), since it needs the freshly computed gradients to exist but has to run before the optimizer actually uses them. I'd use torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ with a max norm like 1.0, which rescales the gradient vector as a whole if its norm exceeds that threshold -- it preserves direction, just caps magnitude -- so one unusually large gradient spike doesn't blow up the weights in a single step.
questions.example:
for x, y in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    preds = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(preds, y)
    loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
    optimizer.step()

Confusing clip_grad_norm_ (rescales by total norm) with clip_grad_value_ (clips each element independently)
Picking a max_norm so small that it suppresses legitimate learning signal, not just outlier spikes
Not realizing clipping is applied across all parameters jointly, not independently per layer by default

questions.title: Diagnosing a Loss That Turns to NaN After a Few Steps
questions.prompt: A training run's loss looks reasonable for the first 20 steps, then suddenly becomes NaN and stays there. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer: NaN loss almost always traces back to a numerical overflow or an invalid math operation (like log(0) or division by zero) somewhere in the forward or backward pass, and once a NaN enters any tensor it propagates through every subsequent computation that touches it, including all future parameter updates, which is why the loss stays NaN forever afterward rather than recovering. The most common concrete causes are: a learning rate that is too high, causing weights to grow until they overflow; mixed-precision (fp16) training where intermediate activations overflow fp16's limited range (resolved via automatic mixed precision's loss scaling, or by checking which specific operation overflows); a numerically unstable operation like an unclipped log or an unprotected division inside a custom loss function; or exploding gradients from a deep or poorly-initialized network. Diagnosis should start by checking at exactly which step and which tensor (loss, a specific layer's activations, or gradients) the NaN first appears, since a NaN in the very first forward pass points to initialization or a numerically unstable input, while a NaN appearing after several healthy steps points to compounding instability like exploding gradients or growing weight magnitudes. torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) helps pinpoint the exact failing operation during backward(). Fixes typically involve lowering the learning rate, adding gradient clipping, double-checking any custom loss math for unguarded log/division, and switching from fp16 to bf16 or using proper loss scaling if mixed precision is the suspect.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is figure out exactly where the NaN first shows up, because once it exists anywhere it poisons everything downstream -- every op that touches a NaN produces another NaN, including every future weight update, which is why it never recovers on its own. If it appears right at step one, I'm suspecting bad initialization or a numerically unstable op on the very first input. If it shows up after 20 healthy-looking steps, that's more consistent with exploding gradients or weights slowly growing until something overflows. I'd turn on torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) to get a stack trace pointing at the exact operation that produced the NaN during backward, rather than guessing. From there the usual suspects are: learning rate too high, so I'd try lowering it and adding gradient clipping as a safety net regardless; if I'm using fp16 mixed precision, I'd check whether an activation is overflowing fp16's narrow range, which usually means I need proper loss scaling or should switch to bf16, which has a much wider range; and if there's any custom loss math, I'd specifically check for an unguarded log of zero or a division that could hit zero. I wouldn't just lower the learning rate and call it fixed without understanding which of these it actually was, because the same symptom can come from very different root causes.

questions.title: Model Accuracy Stuck at Random-Guess Level
questions.prompt: A classifier's training loss is decreasing normally but accuracy stays stuck at exactly what random guessing would give (e.g. 10% for 10 classes). What would you check?
questions.modelAnswer: Decreasing loss but random-level accuracy almost always points to a mismatch between what the loss function is optimizing and what the accuracy metric is measuring, not a fundamentally broken model. The most common cause is a label/prediction misalignment -- the accuracy computation comparing predictions to shuffled or mismatched labels (for instance, computing accuracy on a dataset with a different shuffle order than the one the loss was computed on), or an off-by-one in label indexing. A second common cause is computing accuracy from the wrong tensor, such as taking argmax over the wrong dimension of the logits, which would produce an essentially arbitrary predicted-class assignment unrelated to the model's actual confidence per class. A third is applying softmax before computing accuracy via argmax when it isn't needed (argmax of softmax output equals argmax of raw logits, so this specific case is actually harmless, but is worth ruling out as a red herring during debugging). The fastest way to isolate this is to manually print a handful of raw logits, their argmax, and the corresponding true label side by side for the same batch used in both the loss and accuracy computation, which almost always immediately reveals a misalignment if one exists.
questions.professionalAnswer: When loss is dropping but accuracy is stuck at exactly the random-guess rate, my first assumption isn't that the model is broken -- it's that the accuracy calculation and the loss calculation are somehow looking at different things. The classic culprit is a label alignment bug: maybe the accuracy code pulls labels from a differently-shuffled copy of the dataset than the one used for the loss, or there's an off-by-one in how labels are indexed. The other common one is taking argmax over the wrong axis of the logits tensor, which gives you an essentially random predicted class that has nothing to do with what the model actually thinks. My first move, before changing anything about the model, is to grab one batch, print the raw logits, their argmax, and the true labels side by side, and just eyeball whether the argmax predictions look like they're tracking the labels at all even loosely. That almost always surfaces the misalignment immediately, and it's a much faster diagnosis than tweaking hyperparameters and hoping it goes away.
questions.example: logits.argmax(dim=0) instead of logits.argmax(dim=1) on a (batch, num_classes) tensor silently computes the argmax across the batch dimension instead of the class dimension, producing meaningless predicted classes while the loss (computed correctly against dim=1) keeps decreasing normally.
commonMistakes: Assuming the model architecture itself is broken rather than checking the accuracy computation first
Taking argmax over the wrong tensor dimension
Computing accuracy against a misaligned or differently-shuffled copy of the labels
Changing hyperparameters as a first response instead of inspecting raw predictions vs. labels directly

questions.title: Diagnosing Vanishing Gradients in a Deep MLP
questions.prompt: A 15-layer MLP trained from scratch barely learns anything -- loss decreases extremely slowly and the early layers' weights barely change at all across training. Diagnose and propose fixes.
questions.modelAnswer: Barely-changing early-layer weights in a deep network is the classic signature of vanishing gradients: the chain rule multiplies many layers' local derivatives together during backpropagation, and if those local derivatives are each somewhat less than 1 (which is common with saturating activations like sigmoid or tanh, whose derivative is at most 0.25 and near zero away from the origin), the product shrinks exponentially with depth, so gradients reaching the earliest layers can become vanishingly small by the time they propagate back through 15 layers. The fix set is layered: switching from sigmoid/tanh to ReLU or a variant (which has a derivative of exactly 1 for positive inputs, not shrinking with magnitude) addresses the activation-saturation source directly; adding proper weight initialization (Kaiming/He initialization, matched to the activation function) prevents the problem from being made worse by starting weights at a bad scale; and adding batch normalization or layer normalization between layers directly counteracts the compounding shrinkage by renormalizing activations at every layer, which keeps gradients from systematically shrinking or growing as they propagate. Residual (skip) connections, while more associated with very deep CNNs/transformers, also directly help because they give the gradient a direct additive path around a layer that bypasses the multiplicative shrinkage.
questions.professionalAnswer: The symptom -- early layers barely updating in a 15-layer MLP -- is almost a textbook description of vanishing gradients. Backprop multiplies local derivatives together going backward through each layer, and if those derivatives are each noticeably below 1, which happens with sigmoid or tanh because their derivative tops out around 0.25 and gets near zero away from the center, that product shrinks fast with depth, so by the time the gradient reaches layer 1 of 15 it can be tiny. I'd check the activation functions first; if it's sigmoid or tanh throughout, swapping to ReLU is usually the single highest-leverage fix, since ReLU's derivative is a flat 1 for any positive input instead of shrinking. I'd also check weight initialization -- using a Kaiming/He init matched to the activation, rather than a default or naive initialization, keeps the signal at a reasonable scale from the start instead of compounding the problem. And I'd add batch or layer normalization between layers, which actively renormalizes activations at every layer and directly fights the compounding shrinkage rather than just avoiding making it worse. If it's still an issue after all that, residual connections give gradients an additive shortcut path that sidesteps the multiplicative chain entirely.
questions.example: With tanh (max derivative 0.25) across 15 layers, a naive upper bound on the gradient scaling factor reaching layer 1 is roughly 0.25^14, an extremely small number -- illustrating why even a modest per-layer shrinkage compounds into a severe vanishing-gradient problem at this depth.

questions.title: Training Loss Keeps Falling While Validation Loss Diverges Early
questions.prompt: Training loss keeps decreasing smoothly, but validation loss starts increasing after only a few epochs. What's happening and what would you do?
questions.modelAnswer: This is the classic signature of overfitting: the model is increasingly memorizing patterns specific to the training set, including noise and idiosyncrasies that don't generalize, which keeps driving training loss down while actively hurting performance on unseen validation data. That training loss keeps falling is expected -- the model has enough capacity to keep reducing error on data it has memorized -- while validation loss rising is the signal that this improvement is no longer reflecting genuine learning. Standard fixes include adding or increasing regularization (weight decay, dropout), reducing model capacity if it is clearly oversized for the dataset, using data augmentation to effectively increase the diversity of the training distribution, and using early stopping to halt training at the epoch where validation loss was lowest rather than continuing to the point this question describes. The first overfitting epoch happening 'after only a few epochs' specifically suggests either a very small training dataset relative to model capacity, or too high a learning rate causing rapid memorization, both of which should be checked before assuming regularization alone will fix it.
questions.professionalAnswer: This pattern -- training loss still falling, validation loss turning upward -- is overfitting, not a bug. The model has enough capacity to keep reducing error on the exact training examples it's seen, including their noise, but that memorization stops transferring to data it hasn't seen, which is exactly what rising validation loss is telling you. Given that it's happening after only a few epochs, I'd first check whether the training set is small relative to the model's capacity, or whether the learning rate is high enough that the model is memorizing fast rather than learning generalizable structure -- both point to different first moves. Assuming the basic setup is reasonable, I'd reach for the standard toolkit: add or increase weight decay and dropout, consider whether the model is just bigger than this dataset needs, add data augmentation if applicable to the data type, and set up early stopping so training actually halts near the validation-loss minimum instead of continuing well past it. I wouldn't just let it keep training and pick the final checkpoint -- the useful checkpoint is back near where validation loss bottomed out, not wherever training happened to stop.
questions.example: Epoch 1: train_loss=0.9, val_loss=0.95. Epoch 3: train_loss=0.4, val_loss=0.55. Epoch 6: train_loss=0.1, val_loss=0.9 -- the widening gap after epoch 3 marks where the model started overfitting; the best checkpoint to keep is from around epoch 3, not epoch 6.
commonMistakes: Treating a rising validation loss as a bug to debug rather than the expected signature of overfitting
Not checking dataset size relative to model capacity as a first-pass explanation
Continuing training to the final epoch and keeping that checkpoint instead of the one near the validation minimum
Reaching only for 'more regularization' without first checking whether the learning rate or dataset size is the real driver
keyPoints: Training loss falling while validation loss rises is the classic signature of overfitting
The model is memorizing training-set-specific noise rather than generalizing
Standard fixes: weight decay, dropout, reduced capacity, data augmentation, early stopping
The useful checkpoint is near the validation-loss minimum, not the final training epoch

questions.title: Results Aren't Reproducible Despite Setting a Seed
questions.prompt: A teammate set torch.manual_seed(42) at the top of their script but still gets different results on every run. What are the likely remaining sources of nondeterminism?
questions.modelAnswer: torch.manual_seed() only seeds PyTorch's own CPU random generator; it does not seed numpy's or Python's built-in random module, both of which are commonly used in data loading, augmentation, or custom sampling logic, so any randomness routed through those libraries remains unseeded. It also does not cover torch.cuda's random generator used for GPU operations, which needs torch.cuda.manual_seed_all() separately. Beyond library-level seeding, cuDNN's convolution algorithm auto-tuner (enabled by default via cudnn.benchmark) can select different, individually nondeterministic algorithms run to run for performance reasons, which needs cudnn.deterministic=True and cudnn.benchmark=False to control. Finally, if the DataLoader uses multiple worker processes (num_workers > 0) with any randomness in the data pipeline (shuffling, augmentation), each worker process has its own separate random state that is not automatically seeded by the main process's seed call unless a worker_init_fn explicitly seeds each worker deterministically based on its worker id.
questions.professionalAnswer: manual_seed() alone only covers PyTorch's own CPU random number generator -- it doesn't touch numpy's random state or Python's built-in random module, and a lot of real pipelines use one of those somewhere in data loading or augmentation without anyone noticing. It also doesn't cover the GPU side; you need torch.cuda.manual_seed_all() separately for that. Beyond the seeding itself, there's a sneaky one: cuDNN's convolution algorithm selection can be nondeterministic by default when cudnn.benchmark is on, because it's auto-tuning for speed, not determinism -- you need cudnn.deterministic=True and benchmark=False to shut that off. And if the DataLoader is using multiple worker processes with any random augmentation, each worker has its own separate random state that doesn't automatically inherit the main process's seed -- you need a worker_init_fn that seeds each worker explicitly based on its worker id, or results will vary across runs even with everything else seeded correctly.
questions.example: A training script seeding only torch.manual_seed(42) but using numpy for a random crop augmentation inside a DataLoader with num_workers=4 will get different crops every run, since neither numpy's seed nor each worker's independent random state is controlled by that single call.

Not setting cudnn.deterministic/benchmark, leaving GPU algorithm selection nondeterministic
Not seeding DataLoader worker processes individually when num_workers > 0

GPU operations require a separate torch.cuda.manual_seed_all() call
cudnn.benchmark's auto-tuning can introduce nondeterministic algorithm selection unless disabled
DataLoader worker processes need their own explicit seeding via worker_init_fn

questions.title: Diagnosing a Matrix Multiplication Shape Mismatch
questions.prompt: The following code raises 'RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (32x768 and 512x256)'. Diagnose the likely cause and how you'd fix it.
questions.code:
x = torch.randn(32, 768)
linear = nn.Linear(512, 256)
output = linear(x)
questions.modelAnswer: Matrix multiplication (and nn.Linear internally) requires the inner dimensions to match: x has shape (32, 768) and nn.Linear(512, 256) expects an input with last dimension 512, so the actual multiplication attempted is (32x768) by (768-input-expected-as-512x256), a mismatch between 768 and 512. This is not a bug in the multiplication itself -- it is almost always upstream, either the Linear layer was constructed with the wrong input dimension (should be nn.Linear(768, 256) to match x's actual feature dimension), or x itself has an unexpected shape because an earlier layer or reshape produced 768 features instead of the 512 the rest of the model expects. The fix is to trace backward from this error to find which side is actually wrong: print x.shape right before this line and compare it against what the model's architecture assumes the input dimension should be.
questions.professionalAnswer: nn.Linear(512, 256) is expecting its input's last dimension to be 512, but x has last dimension 768, so the fix depends on which one is actually correct for this model. If x really should have 768 features at this point, the Linear layer was constructed with the wrong in_features and should be nn.Linear(768, 256). If the architecture genuinely expects 512 features here, then something upstream -- maybe an earlier layer's output size, or a reshape/flatten operation -- is producing 768 instead of 512, and that's where I'd actually go looking, not at this line itself. I'd just print x.shape right before this call and trace back through whatever produced x to find where the dimension diverged from what was intended.
questions.example:
# If x should have 768 features:
linear = nn.Linear(768, 256)
output = linear(x)  # works

# If x should have 512 features, trace back to find why it has 768 instead

Guessing a fix without checking which side (the layer's in_features or x's actual shape) is the one that's wrong
Not printing the actual shapes involved before attempting a fix
Assuming the fix is always to change the Linear layer, when the real bug might be further upstream
keyPoints: nn.Linear requires its input's last dimension to match in_features exactly
The error means the actual input shape and the layer's expected shape disagree
The fix requires determining which side is correct, not guessing
Printing the actual tensor shape right before the failing line is the fastest diagnostic step

questions.title: Handling a GPU Out-of-Memory Error Mid-Training
questions.prompt: Training crashes with CUDA out of memory after running fine for several epochs. What would you check and what are your options for fixing it without a hardware upgrade?
questions.modelAnswer: If training ran fine for several epochs before crashing, the most likely cause is not a simple static memory shortage (which would fail immediately) but something growing over time, such as accidentally retaining the computation graph across iterations (e.g. appending loss directly instead of loss.item() into a logging list, which keeps every historical graph alive in memory) or a batch with unusually large inputs (e.g. one unusually long sequence in a variable-length dataset) arriving later in training. If the crash is consistent and immediate rather than growing, the simplest fixes are reducing batch size, enabling gradient accumulation to simulate a larger effective batch size without the memory cost, switching to mixed-precision (fp16/bf16) training which roughly halves activation memory, and enabling gradient checkpointing (trading recomputation time for memory by not storing all intermediate activations). Diagnosis should start by checking whether memory usage was growing steadily across epochs (pointing to a leak like the loss.item() issue) versus whether it was flat until a sudden large batch or sequence (pointing to a data-dependent spike), which can be checked via torch.cuda.memory_summary() or similar monitoring.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that this ran fine for several epochs before crashing is the important clue -- a true static memory shortage would fail on the very first batch, not several epochs in. That pattern makes me suspect something growing over time, and the single most common cause I'd check first is whether loss (the full tensor, not loss.item()) is getting appended into some logging list -- that silently keeps every historical computation graph alive in memory, and it compounds epoch after epoch until it finally runs out. The other common cause is a late-arriving unusually large batch or sequence in a variable-length dataset. I'd check torch.cuda.memory_summary() across a few epochs to see whether usage is flat-then-spiking (data-dependent) or steadily climbing (a leak). If it's a genuine memory ceiling rather than a leak, my options without new hardware are: reduce batch size, use gradient accumulation to recover the effective batch size I lost, switch to fp16/bf16 mixed precision which roughly halves activation memory, and use gradient checkpointing to trade some recomputation time for a lot less memory held at once.
questions.example:
losses = []
for x, y in loader:
    ...
    loss = loss_fn(preds, y)
    losses.append(loss)  # BUG: keeps the full computation graph alive every iteration
    # fix: losses.append(loss.item())
commonMistakes: Assuming any OOM is a static capacity problem rather than checking whether memory usage was growing over time
Appending the full loss tensor instead of loss.item() into a logging list, silently leaking the computation graph
Jumping straight to reducing batch size without first checking for a leak
Not knowing gradient accumulation and gradient checkpointing as memory-saving options besides reducing batch size
keyPoints: A crash after several working epochs suggests something growing over time, not a static shortage
Appending full loss tensors (instead of .item()) into logs is a common silent memory leak
torch.cuda.memory_summary() helps distinguish a leak from a data-dependent spike
Fixes for a genuine memory ceiling: smaller batch size, gradient accumulation, mixed precision, gradient checkpointing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about delayed-crash timing pointing to a growing leak
